topic.title: Variants
topic.p: variant<A, B, ...> is a value type that stores one declared option and its value. It maps to vl::Variant in generated C++. The active option is preserved when the value is copied, passed through reflection, or stored in a typed collection.

topic.title: Type identity and valid options
topic.p: A variant requires at least two valid value types. Options are ordered: variant<int, string> and variant<string, int> are different Workflow types. Resolved aliases refer to the same option, so string and system::String cannot both appear. The target architecture determines what int and uint mean.
An option cannot be void or itself be a variant. A variant itself cannot have a pointer or optional decoration. Collections of variant elements are supported.

Options must also produce distinct native C++ alternatives. For example, int[] and string[] both map to Ptr<IValueList>, so they cannot be two options in one variant. This restriction does not make those two list types equal elsewhere in Workflow. Function signatures in Func and enumerable element types in LazyList remain distinct native types.
A native untyped collection option retains its declared metadata. Reflection does not inspect a Ptr<IValueList> payload to turn it into an exact int[] option.

topic.title: Construction, assignment and conversion

ul.li: cast VARIANT value and value of VARIANT select the exact declared type of a nonvariant value. Numeric, inheritance, pointer-ownership and optional conversions do not make an option match.
cast OPTION value requires that exact option to be declared. It throws when a different option is active.
cast TARGET_VARIANT value requires a nonempty intersection of option types. It throws when the active option is outside that intersection.
value of TARGET_VARIANT requires every source option to occur in the target. It preserves the active option and permits reordering.

topic.p: For the example above, cast string number is a runtime failure: string is declared, but int is active. A cast to an option that is not declared is a compiler error. Bare null and other expressions needing an expected type cannot choose an option implicitly; first give the payload an explicit type.

This declaration is rejected because a variant does not implicitly convert to object:
func f(x:variant<int, string>):void { var y:object = x; }

topic.title: Weak casts, null and defaults
topic.p: Null does not erase the active option. Strong extraction of a matching null pointer or empty optional succeeds; extraction of another declared option throws even when both payloads would be null. Likewise, a base-pointer option containing a derived object remains the base-pointer option.

is null and is not null require at least one null-bearing option and inspect the active payload. They do not test whether the outer variant box exists. A compiler-generated default, including an unassigned struct field, selects the first declared option and uses that option's default value. Thus a default variant<int, string> contains integer zero; a default variant<int?, string> contains an empty optional tagged as int?.

topic.title: Extracting the active payload as object
topic.p: This operator has the same precedence as unary +, -, not and cast. Unary operators group from right to left, so cast int variant in number first extracts the payload and then casts it. Calls, indexing and member access bind more tightly: variant in values[0].Get() extracts the returned variant. Use parentheses around a lower-precedence operand or around the extraction before a type test, such as (variant in value) is null.

Extraction removes exactly one variant layer. If an object option contains a variant box supplied by native C++ code, the result is that inner box. It is not recursively extracted, and its static type remains object.

topic.title: The object option
topic.p: An explicit object option takes precedence. Converting an object-typed value to such a variant selects that option without inspecting the payload. Casting that variant to object extracts only an active object option; another active option causes a runtime failure.

topic.title: Comparison and other operations
topic.p: Comparison is a partial ordering. Unordered payloads, including NaN, produce false for == and all relational operators, and true for !=. Pointer payloads retain the existing pointer-identity semantics.

Extract an option before arithmetic, logical operations, indexing, invocation or member access. Type tests with is TYPE or is not TYPE, and variant type queries, are unsupported. Reading a variant-valued field or property is supported; extracting a value makes a copy, and writing back requires assigning a complete valid variant.

topic.title: Bindings and RPC
topic.p: A binding publishes through ValueChanged(object). A direct variant result is therefore rejected. Use bind(variant in source.Value) to publish the active payload as object, or produce another allowed nonvariant result. Observing and caching a variant while producing such a result is supported.

RPC does not support variants, including variants contained in collection arguments, optional wrappers or struct fields. An extracted payload can be serialized only if its value is supported by RPC. A variant box supplied by native C++ code remains unsupported, including a box nested inside an extracted object payload.
